name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
title: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
answer: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to rank or classify large document sets for litigation and investigation, most often to separate responsive material from the rest before a review team sees it. The practice sits inside e-discovery, alongside keyword search, deduplication and manual review, and it applies to email, chat, office files and scanned paper alike. It matters because document populations in modern matters routinely run into the millions, and linear review of that volume is slow and expensive.

sections.body: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to rank or classify large document sets for litigation and investigation, most often to separate responsive material from the rest before a review team sees it. The practice sits inside e-discovery, alongside keyword search, deduplication and manual review, and it applies to email, chat, office files and scanned paper alike. It matters because document populations in modern matters routinely run into the millions, and linear review of that volume is slow and expensive.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a review platform that ingests documents, extracts text and metadata, and hosts the coding interface, with processing engines handling optical character recognition for scans and near-duplicate detection. Underneath sit search and analytics layers, typically Elasticsearch or similar indexing, plus storage for the document set and its extracted text. Model training and scoring may run inside the platform or on separate compute, and the outputs are written back as per-document scores and tags that reviewers and counsel can sort and filter.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts with a seed set of documents coded by a human reviewer, which trains a classifier to score the remaining population by likely responsiveness. The team then reviews the highest-scoring documents, adds those judgments back into training, and repeats until the ranking stabilises, a loop known as continuous active learning. Recall is estimated against a random or statistically drawn sample, and the resulting metrics are documented so the process can be defended. Simple keyword and Boolean search usually remains in the mix, either to build the seed set or to catch material the model ranks low.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Courts have generally accepted predictive coding where the process is transparent, the seed set is sound and the parties agree on validation, and several decisions have addressed how far a producing party must disclose its methodology. Proportionality and reasonableness under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure shape how much review is enough, and privilege review still requires care because a model that ranks responsiveness does not automatically protect privileged material. Provenance matters throughout: teams keep training logs, seed set records, scoring versions and recall estimates so that opposing counsel and the court can examine how the set was built.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration of review into case strategy, with active learning as the default rather than a novelty and with generative models increasingly used to summarise documents and draft privilege logs. Expect more attention to validation standards, to the disclosure of model behaviour, and to how review outputs are explained to courts that are still building familiarity with the technique. The site currently tracks 152 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 7,169 state AI bills, a reminder that the surrounding law is moving at least as fast as the tooling.
